questions.question: Q1. Write the ideal gas equation and the molecular form.
questions.answer: PV = nRT = (N/N_A)RT = Nk_BT, where k_B = R/N_A is Boltzmann's constant (1.38×10⁻²³ J/K). It is valid at high pressure & temperature where intermolecular forces and molecular volume are negligible.

questions.question: Q2. State the ideal gas assumptions.
questions.answer: (i) Molecules are point masses with no volume. (ii) No intermolecular forces except during perfectly elastic collisions. (iii) Collisions with walls are elastic. (iv) Obeys PV = nRT.
questions.shortcut: Point particles, elastic, no forces → ideal gas.
questions.example: Real gases approach ideal at low P, high T.

questions.question: Q3. Find the volume of 2 moles of gas at 300 K and 2 atm (R = 0.0821 L·atm/mol·K).
questions.answer: V = nRT/P = 2×0.0821×300/2 = 24.6 L. ▥ 13.1–13.2 Ideal Gas Equation & Molecular Properties  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Ideal Gas vs Real Gas Isobaric vs Isothermal Processes ▣ 13.3–13.6 Kinetic Theory & RMS Speed

questions.question: Q4. Derive the expression for the pressure exerted by an ideal gas (kinetic theory).
questions.answer: A molecule of mass m, speed v, hitting a wall reverses momentum, giving Δp per molecule and N molecules in volume V gives P = ⅓(Nm/molecule)⟨v²⟩ = ⅓(ρ)v_rms². Using N molecules, P = (1/3)(N m v_rms²)/V = (2/3)(N/V)⟨K⟩.
questions.example: Pressure arises from wall collisions, not from gravity.

questions.question: Q5. Relate temperature to average translational kinetic energy.
questions.answer: The mean translational kinetic energy per molecule is ⟨K⟩ = 3/2 k_BT; per mole ⟨K⟩ = 3/2 RT. Hence temperature is a direct measure of average translational KE.
questions.shortcut: ⟨K⟩ = 3/2 kT per molecule; 3/2 RT per mole.

questions.question: Q6. Define root-mean-square speed and give its formula.
questions.answer: v_rms = √(⟨v²⟩) = √(3RT/M) for a gas of molar mass M (or √(3kT/m) per molecule). It is the speed that gives the same kinetic energy as the average.
questions.example: H₂ (light) has larger v_rms than O₂ at same T.

questions.question: Q7. Find the v_rms of nitrogen (M=28 g/mol) at 300 K.
Q8. State two gas kinetic properties that depend on temperature.
questions.answer: Mean translational KE and v_rms both depend on absolute temperature (∝ T and √T respectively), while the distribution of molecular speeds (Maxwell-Boltzmann) broadens with increasing T. ▥ 13.3–13.6 Kinetic Theory & RMS Speed  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Three Molecular Speeds (mean, rms, most-probable) ▣ 13.7 Heat Capacities
questions.example: Heating a gas widens the speed spread.

questions.question: Q9. Define molar heat capacities C_v and C_p; state Mayer's relation.
questions.answer: C_v is heat to raise 1 mole by 1 K at constant volume; C_p at constant pressure. Mayer's relation: C_p − C_v = R. For monatomic ideal gas C_v = 3R/2, C_p = 5R/2.
questions.shortcut: C_p − C_v = R ; monatomic: C_v=3R/2, C_p=5R/2.
questions.example: C_p > C_v because part of the heat goes into work at constant P.

questions.question: Q10. Why is C_p greater than C_v?
questions.answer: At constant pressure, part of the supplied heat does expansion work (PΔV), so more heat is required to raise the temperature than at constant volume: C_p = C_v + R (Mayer).
questions.shortcut: C_p = C_v + R (heat does expansion work).
questions.example: Raising 1 mole at constant P needs more heat.

questions.question: Q11. Compute C_v and C_p for a monatomic ideal gas (R = 8.314).
questions.answer: C_v = 3R/2 = 12.47 J/mol·K; C_p = 5R/2 = 20.79 J/mol·K; difference = R = 8.314 J/mol·K.

questions.question: Q12. Explain heat capacity of solids using the equipartition/Debye model (qualitatively).
questions.answer: In a solid each atom vibrates with 3 translational + 3 rotational DOF, giving C_v ≈ 3R per mole at high T (Dulong–Petit). At low T the heat capacity falls ~T³ (Debye), because phonon modes freeze out. ▥ 13.7 Heat Capacities  —  Compare / Contrast Tables C_V vs C_P and γ for Gases PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: Solids ≈ 3R/mol at high T; ∝T³ at low T.
questions.example: Ice near 0 K has much lower c than near room T.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive the pressure exerted by a gas from the kinetic theory.
theoryItems.answer: A molecule of mass m, velocity components (vₓ,v_y,v_z) hitting a wall reverses vₓ; momentum change per collision = 2mvₓ. For N molecules in volume V, the mean pressure P = ⅓(ρ)v_rms² = (1/3)(Nm/M)⟨v²⟩. This links pressure to molecular KE.
theoryItems.example: Pressure is due to molecular impacts on the walls.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T2. Derive the mean translational kinetic energy per molecule.
theoryItems.answer: From PV = (1/3)Nm⟨v²⟩/V and PV = Nk_BT, equating gives (1/2)m⟨v²⟩ = (3/2)k_BT. So the mean translational KE per molecule = 3/2 k_BT; per mole = 3/2 RT.
theoryItems.example: Temperature is a direct measure of average molecular KE.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T3. Derive the molar heat capacities of an ideal gas and Mayer's relation.
theoryItems.answer: For a monatomic ideal gas, by equipartition each translational DOF contributes (1/2)R, so C_v = 3R/2. At constant pressure extra energy does work, so C_p = C_v + R = 5R/2. Mayer's relation: C_p − C_v = R.
theoryItems.example: C_p > C_v because part of the heat does expansion work.

theoryItems.question: [State] T4. State the ideal gas equation and the law of Boyle and Charles combined.
theoryItems.answer: The ideal gas equation is PV = nRT. Boyle's law (PV = const at constant T) and Charles's law (V/T = const at constant P) combine with Avogadro's law to give PV = nRT; molecularly, PV = Nk_BT.
theoryItems.shortcut: PV = nRT = Nk_B T ; k_B = R/N_A.
theoryItems.example: At fixed T, PV is constant; at fixed P, V ∝ T.

theoryItems.question: [Compare] T5. Compare the heat capacities of gases and solids.
theoryItems.answer: Gases have well-defined C_v and C_p (C_p > C_v by R), with values depending on molecular complexity (more DOF for polyatomic). Solids have C_v ≈ 3R per mole at room temperature (Dulong-Petit) but fall as T³ at very low T.
theoryItems.shortcut: Gas: C_p > C_v; Solid: ~3R at high T, ∝T³ at low T.
theoryItems.example: Water has a much higher c than metals.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain root-mean-square speed and how it depends on temperature and molar mass.
theoryItems.answer: v_rms = √⟨v²⟩ = √(3k_BT/m) = √(3RT/M). It increases with √T and decreases with √M: at the same temperature, lighter gases have higher v_rms. The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution broadens with T.
theoryItems.example: H₂ (light) has a larger v_rms than O₂ at the same T.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain the kinetic-molecular model of an ideal gas.
theoryItems.answer: Assumptions: (i) many small particles in constant random motion; (ii) collisions with the walls and each other are perfectly elastic; (iii) no intermolecular forces except at collision; (iv) particle volume is negligible. These give PV = Nk_BT and connect pressure to molecular KE.
theoryItems.shortcut: Point particles, elastic, no forces → PV=Nk_BT.
theoryItems.example: Real gases approach this at low P, high T.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T8. Explain the equipartition theorem and the Dulong-Petit law for solids.
theoryItems.answer: Equipartition: each quadratic degree of freedom carries (1/2)k_BT of energy. For a monatomic gas: 3 translational DOF → (3/2)k_BT per molecule. For a solid, each atom vibrates in 3 directions (kinetic + potential) → 3k_BT → C_v ≈ 3R per mole (Dulong-Petit) at high T.
theoryItems.example: Dulong-Petit explains the ~constant solid specific heat.

theoryItems.question: [Why] T9. Why does the heat capacity of a solid decrease at very low temperature?
theoryItems.answer: At low T, many vibrational (phonon) modes are frozen out, so fewer modes are available to absorb energy; the heat capacity falls roughly as T³ (Debye's law), instead of the Dulong-Petit 3R.
theoryItems.shortcut: Low T → phonons freeze out → C_v ∝ T³.
theoryItems.example: Ice near 0 K has a much lower c than at room temperature.

theoryItems.question: [Numerical] T10. Find the rms speed of oxygen (M = 32 g/mol) at 300 K and the mean KE per molecule.

▣ 13.1–13.2 Ideal Gas Equation & Molecular Properties
Q1. Write the ideal gas equation and the molecular form.

Answer:  PV = nRT = (N/N_A)RT = Nk_BT, where k_B = R/N_A is Boltzmann's constant (1.38×10⁻²³ J/K). It is valid at high pressure & temperature where intermolecular forces and molecular volume are negligible.
⚡ Shortcut:  PV = Nk_B T ; k_B = R/N_A.
Example:  1 mole: PV = RT.
Q2. State the ideal gas assumptions.
Answer:  (i) Molecules are point masses with no volume. (ii) No intermolecular forces except during perfectly elastic collisions. (iii) Collisions with walls are elastic. (iv) Obeys PV = nRT.
⚡ Shortcut:  Point particles, elastic, no forces → ideal gas.
Example:  Real gases approach ideal at low P, high T.
Q3. Find the volume of 2 moles of gas at 300 K and 2 atm (R = 0.0821 L·atm/mol·K).
⚡ Shortcut:  V = nRT/P.
Example:  ≈ 24.6 L.

Q4. Derive the expression for the pressure exerted by an ideal gas (kinetic theory).

Answer:  A molecule of mass m, speed v, hitting a wall reverses momentum, giving Δp per molecule and N molecules in volume V gives P = ⅓(Nm/molecule)⟨v²⟩ = ⅓(ρ)v_rms². Using N molecules, P = (1/3)(N m v_rms²)/V = (2/3)(N/V)⟨K⟩.
⚡ Shortcut:  P = ⅓(Nm/M)v_rms² = ⅓ρv_rms² ; P ∝ T.
Example:  Pressure arises from wall collisions, not from gravity.
Q5. Relate temperature to average translational kinetic energy.
Answer:  The mean translational kinetic energy per molecule is ⟨K⟩ = 3/2 k_BT; per mole ⟨K⟩ = 3/2 RT. Hence temperature is a direct measure of average translational KE.
⚡ Shortcut:  ⟨K⟩ = 3/2 kT per molecule; 3/2 RT per mole.
Example:  Higher T → faster molecules.
Q6. Define root-mean-square speed and give its formula.
Answer:  v_rms = √(⟨v²⟩) = √(3RT/M) for a gas of molar mass M (or √(3kT/m) per molecule). It is the speed that gives the same kinetic energy as the average.
⚡ Shortcut:  v_rms = √(3RT/M); heavier M → slower.
Example:  H₂ (light) has larger v_rms than O₂ at same T.
Q7. Find the v_rms of nitrogen (M=28 g/mol) at 300 K.
⚡ Shortcut:  v_rms = √(3RT/M).
Example:  ≈ 520 m/s.
Q8. State two gas kinetic properties that depend on temperature.
Answer:  Mean translational KE and v_rms both depend on absolute temperature (∝ T and √T respectively), while the distribution of molecular speeds (Maxwell-Boltzmann) broadens with increasing T.
⚡ Shortcut:  ⟨K⟩ ∝ T ; v_rms ∝ √T.
Example:  Heating a gas widens the speed spread.

▣ 13.7 Heat Capacities
Q9. Define molar heat capacities C_v and C_p; state Mayer's relation.
Answer:  C_v is heat to raise 1 mole by 1 K at constant volume; C_p at constant pressure. Mayer's relation: C_p − C_v = R. For monatomic ideal gas C_v = 3R/2, C_p = 5R/2.
⚡ Shortcut:  C_p − C_v = R ; monatomic: C_v=3R/2, C_p=5R/2.
Example:  C_p > C_v because part of the heat goes into work at constant P.
Q10. Why is C_p greater than C_v?
Answer:  At constant pressure, part of the supplied heat does expansion work (PΔV), so more heat is required to raise the temperature than at constant volume: C_p = C_v + R (Mayer).
⚡ Shortcut:  C_p = C_v + R (heat does expansion work).
Example:  Raising 1 mole at constant P needs more heat.
Q11. Compute C_v and C_p for a monatomic ideal gas (R = 8.314).
Answer:  C_v = 3R/2 = 12.47 J/mol·K; C_p = 5R/2 = 20.79 J/mol·K; difference = R = 8.314 J/mol·K.
⚡ Shortcut:  C_v=12.5, C_p=20.8 J/mol·K.
Example:  He/Ar (monatomic) use these values.
Q12. Explain heat capacity of solids using the equipartition/Debye model (qualitatively).

Answer:  In a solid each atom vibrates with 3 translational + 3 rotational DOF, giving C_v ≈ 3R per mole at high T (Dulong–Petit). At low T the heat capacity falls ~T³ (Debye), because phonon modes freeze out.
⚡ Shortcut:  Solids ≈ 3R/mol at high T; ∝T³ at low T.
Example:  Ice near 0 K has much lower c than near room T.
